aitrusis-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous and mixed forests with oak and hazel, parks
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, sometimes larger, faintly zoned, matt, pale ochre, dirty yellowish ochre-brown, with a delicate violet tinge. Gills thick, pinkish, ochre-coloured, subdecurrent. Stem 3-8x0.3-2 cm, yellowish. Flesh white, turning yellow when cut or broken, with a pleasant fruity smell, not bitter; the milk is white, acrid-tasting, and does not change colour.
Characteristic features: cap the colour of an old nutshell; especially fond of the company of hazel. Usually grows in small numbers of fruiting bodies, in forests and parks. Edible, common.

Fruiting bodies large. Cap 7-15 (20) cm across, fleshy, flattened, with a blunt umbo, matt, greyish-brownish, leather-brown, slightly velvety. Gills crowded, narrow, pale cream, greyish, yellowish-brownish, subdecurrent, adnate. Stem 4—7x3-4 cm, firm, cottony inside, greyish in colour. Flesh thick, soft, greyish-yellowish, with a pleasant taste and a woody smell. Characteristic features: cap greyish yellowish-brownish, fleshy, large, semi-convex. Grows in small groups, rarely singly, under spruces in coniferous forests, most often in old spruce stands. Edible, uncommon.

ametistine-lakabude.features: Spores spiny (spines up to 2 pm long), round
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap grows up to 5-6 cm across, usually 3-4 cm. Flattened-convex, matt, finely scaly, greyish-blue with a violet tinge. Gills thick, distant, violet, bluish-violet, adnate or subdecurrent. Stem up to 10 cm long and 1 cm thick, the colour of the cap, violet-fibrous at the base. Flesh pale violet, thin, with a mushroomy smell and taste. Characteristic features: greyish-blue mushrooms with a violet tinge. Grows in small groups, sometimes of several dozen fruiting bodies; likes mossy, grassy places. Edible. Uncommon.

auksavirse-skujagalve.habitat: On trunks, branches, stumps and snags of deciduous trees
auksavirse-skujagalve.features: Cap yellowish-brown with brown scales, stem with a ring or its remnant
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5-10 (13) cm across, rarely larger, fleshy, yellow, brownish-yellow, sticky, covered with brownish, appressed scales. Gills cream, later yellowish-brown, greenish-brown. Stem 4-8 (10)x0.5-2 (3) cm, hard, woody, smooth or roughened, with a cobweb-like ring-shaped remnant of the veil. Characteristic features: slimy cap with brown scales on a yellow background, flesh not bitter, yellowish. Grows in small groups in parks, forests, along roadsides, in squares, on deciduous trees, even in orchards on damaged parts of apple trees. Edible, of low value. Common.

auksakotis-aksombaravykis.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, parks
auksakotis-aksombaravykis.features: Cap surface cracked, stem streaked with red
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3—8 cm across. Surface velvety, greenish-greyish-brown, usually cracked and fissured, with red flesh showing in the cracks and fissures. Stem 3-7 cm long, 1-2 cm thick, yellowish, red or streaked pinkish in the lower part, sometimes all over. Characteristic features: flesh slowly turns blue when broken or cut, with a pleasant smell and taste. Grows singly. Likes the company of oak and hazel. Edible, not rare. Used fresh or dried.

auksiskoji-umede.habitat: Birch woods, damp pine forests with birch, black alder woods
auksiskoji-umede.features: Cap and gills greenish-yellow, grows under birches and alders
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 5-12 cm across, convex-flattened, eventually horizontal, slightly depressed or faintly convex; the cuticle peels easily; beautifully yellow, greenish-yellow, chrome yellow. Gills cream, later yellow-ochre, blackening, adnexed. Stem 4-10x0.5-2 cm, white, turning greyish and blackish with age. Flesh white, turning grey and blackish when broken, not bitter. Characteristic features: flesh turns greyish and blackish when cut or broken, not bitter in taste. Grows in groups. Edible, tasty, valuable. Common. Found abundantly in the damper pine forests of the Curonian Spit.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-10 cm across, convex, later broadly flattened, irregularly flattened, slightly depressed; the cuticle is adnate and peels with difficulty; yellowish-red, golden, apricot, brick-coloured. Young gills cream, later yellowish, yellow, broad, adnate. Stem 3-9x 1-2.5 cm, white, yellowish when old. Flesh thick, firm, slightly bitter in taste. Characteristic features: gills and stem yellowish, spores large. Grows singly or in small groups, likes calcareous soil. Edible, but very rare. Protected.

auksuotoji-smulkiazvyne.habitat: Forest edges, woodland margins, scrub, ditch sides, grassy lake shores, riverbanks
auksuotoji-smulkiazvyne.features: Yellow, golden, robust fruiting bodies, grows in groups
desc: Fruiting bodies large, robust. Cap up to 35 cm across and larger, velvety, finely granular, scaly, golden in colour. Young gills covered by a leathery yellow granular veil, later free, yellowish-brown, narrow. Stem 8—15 (20)x2-6 cm, thickening towards the base, with a membranous yellow ring, above which it is whitish, yellowish, smooth, and below it granular, scaly, the colour of the cap. Flesh yellowish, thick, without a particular smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fleshy, large fruiting bodies, finely scaly, granular, with a prominent granular yellow ring. Grows in large groups, sometimes in rings, on peaty soils. Edible. Common. Large caps and stems are not to be eaten.

avine-dirvapinte.habitat: Old coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, especially spruce stands
desc: Fruiting bodies massive, fleshy. Cap 5-12 (15) cm, irregularly shaped, surface white, greyish, greyish-yellowish, fissured, cracked. Tubes white, yellowish when old. Stem 3-5 (7)x1—3 cm, sometimes eccentric, white, firm. Flesh white, soft, mild in taste, with a pleasant smell. Characteristic features: a mushroom of old-growth forests (spruce and pine stands), greyish-yellowish fruiting bodies, several fused at the stems. Grows in small groups, likes calcareous soil. Edible when young. Rare. The Fused Polypore (Albatrellus confluens) is very similar to the Sheep Polypore, only its caps and stems are fused even more into clumps, and the stem is branched. Edible. Rare.

azuoline-kepena.habitat: On trunks of old oaks, rarely at their base
azuoline-kepena.features: Fruiting bodies reddish-brown, fleshy, not woody, tongue-shaped
desc: An annual fungus. Young fruiting bodies are knob-shaped, later spatula- or tongue-shaped, attached to the tree by the margin or by a short lateral end - a stem. Young fruiting bodies are fleshy, elastic, juicy, later fibrous; they grow up to 20 cm across and 6 cm thick and much larger; the surface is orange-red, the colour of blood, meat, old brown mushrooms, liver. Tubes up to 1.5 cm long, yellowish, darkening when pressed. Flesh fleshy, juicy, saturated with reddish juice, sour in taste. Characteristic features: a mushroom of soft, juicy consistency. Grows in parks and forests on oaks, rarely on other deciduous trees. Causes active brown rot of wood. Edible. Not rare. Protected.

azuolyninis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Oak woods, deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests
desc: Fruiting bodies robust, fleshy. Cap grows up to 20 cm across, fibrous, scaly, orange-brown, reddish-brown. Tubes and pores grey. Stem 10—15 (20)x2-4 (5) cm, white, when young with white, later reddish-violet fibrils. Flesh white, firm, thick, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: grows only under oaks, less often under beeches; when pressed or cut, the white flesh turns pinkish, eventually becoming greyish-violet. Usually appears singly or a few fruiting bodies together, in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests (under oaks). Edible, very valuable. Found much more rarely than the Orange Birch Bolete and the Blackish-scaled Bolete.

baltagauris-piengrybis.habitat: Deciduous forests, especially boggy, grassy birch woods
baltagauris-piengrybis.features: Similar to the Woolly Milkcap, but its fruiting bodies are smaller, white, yellowish
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-7 (8) cm across, white, yellowish when old, fibrous, the margins especially shaggy. Gills white, later cream, crowded, adnate, subdecurrent. Stem 2-4x0.5—1.5 cm, tapering towards the base, white. Characteristic features: cap margins shaggy, flesh white, burning in taste, the milk is white and does not change colour; likes wet, boggy, grassy places. Edible. Common. Very similar to a faded Woolly Milkcap.

baltasis-bals-vis.habitat: Roadsides, parks, gardens, fallow land, fields, squares
baltasis-bals-vis.features: Gills white, only turning brownish when old, spores broadly elliptical
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5—10 cm across, when young elongated bell-shaped, later bluntly conical, eventually flattened, with an indistinct blunt umbo, white, later cream, fibrous, scaly; margins bent downwards with ragged remnants of the partial veil. Gills white, when old pale pinkish-rose, crowded, broad, soft, free. Stem 5-10x1-2 cm, thickening towards the base, with a white ring, white, brownish in the lower part, sometimes bulbous at the base. Flesh fairly thick, firm, white, not changing colour, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: similar to white field mushrooms (Agaricus), differs in its white, brownish gills. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Edible. Common.

baravykas.habitat: Forests: under pines, oaks, spruces, birches, beeches
desc: The most valuable edible mushroom, made famous in proverbs, fairy tales, poems and songs. It has enchanted mushroom pickers with its beauty - which is why it is the king of mushrooms. And who does not long to find it when going mushroom picking? It always has the most visible place in the basket! A mushroom known to every mushroom picker.

The Polish professor Karpinski managed to grow it in a test tube; research continues, but so far it is not yet cultivated artificially. It is not only the most nutritious mushroom, but also one with medicinal properties.
Characteristic features: forms mycorrhiza with several tree species; the stem has a network (reticulum) only in its upper part.
Grows large (in Lithuania up to 3 kg). In great demand on the local and foreign markets.

baravykas-paazuolis.habitat: Deciduous forests, parks with oak, linden, birch
desc: Fruiting bodies robust, fleshy. Cap grows up to 20 cm across, velvety, brownish-grey, dirty, softly greenish-brown, with a faint yellowish tinge. Tubes up to 2 cm long, yellow; pores red, brownish-red. Stem massive, up to 15 cm long and 5 cm thick, orange-red, with a black, coarse network. Flesh yellowish, later yellow, turning blue when broken, then fading to bluish, not bitter. Characteristic features: the tubes and the flesh of the cap and stem turn blue when cut, later fading. Grows singly or in small groups. Likes light, grassy, calcareous places and the company of oak. Edible when well boiled, provided no alcoholic drinks are consumed. Not rare.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 3-10 cm across, rarely larger, flattened, with an umbo; its ochre surface is reddish-brown fibrous and scaly, the margins paler, densely hairy, bearded. Gills crowded, yellowish, cream, adnate. Stem 4-10x0.3-2 cm, of uniform thickness, firm, fibrous, finely scaly, the colour of the cap or paler. Flesh whitish, brownish, with an unpleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies reddish-brown, shaggy. Grows singly or in small groups in coniferous forests, especially spruce stands. Edible when well boiled, of low value.

berzyninis-baravykas.habitat: Only under birches, light, grassy places
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap white, whitish, grows up to 15 cm across. Tubes 1-2.5 cm long, white, when old yellowish-greenish. Stem 5-12x2-3 cm in size, when young bulging, when old cylindrical, white, brownish, with a pale network. Flesh white, not changing colour when cut, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: likes open, light habitats. Grows in forests, parks, even farmsteads, under solitary birches. A very tasty mushroom, loved by mushroom pickers (fresh, dried, pickled, frozen). Uncommon.

bevainike-musmire.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, often boggy places
bevainike-musmire.features: Fruiting bodies grey, yellowish-brownish-grey, stem without a ring
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-9 (12) cm across, but also grows larger, grey, ash-grey, surface smooth, without scales, in rare cases with white remnants of the veil, margins grooved. Gills white, broad, free. Stem up to 20 cm long and 1-2 cm thick, without a ring, white, grey, paler than the cap, at the base with a loose, large, unattached, white or greyish volva. Flesh white, soft, thick, without a particular smell. Characteristic features: cap without scales, the grey colour of the fruiting body varies, even to white. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, but of low value and not advisable to collect, because it resembles poisonous Amanitas. Not rare, quite widespread in places.

blunkancioji-umede.features: Flesh blackens when cut and with age, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5—12 cm across and larger, domed, when old convex-flattened, the centre slightly depressed, margins lobed and grooved; the cuticle peels to the middle; slimy in damp weather, shiny when dry, yellowish-brown, orange-red, fading to brownish. Gills yellowish-white, when old yellow, greyish-blackish. Stem 5-10x1-2.5 cm, white, when old blackish. Flesh white, firm, thick, honey-like in taste, without a particular smell, blackening. Characteristic features: cap from yellowish-brownish to orange-red, fading; gills and stem turn grey and black with age. Grows in groups, sometimes large ones. A very good edible mushroom. Common. An important enzyme, russulin, has been isolated from this brittlegill; it is suitable for making enzyme-ripened cheeses and fully replaces rennin obtained from young lambs and calves.

bohemiskasis-auksliavarpis.features: Stem 2—3 times longer than the cap, which is wrinkled in a convoluted way
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 2—3 cm tall and 2—4 cm across, bell-shaped, irregularly longitudinally wrinkled in a convoluted way, yellowish-brown, when old dark brown, margins free. Stem 7-12x1.5-3 cm, whitish, pale yellowish-brown, smooth, faintly fibrous. Flesh whitish, thin, brittle. Characteristic features: cap wrinkled in a convoluted way, its margins flared, not attached to the stem; flesh yellowish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Grows singly or in groups on river slopes; likes humus-rich soil and the company of aspen. Edible. Uncommon. Listed in the Red Data Book of Lithuania.

Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap grows up to 30 cm across. In Lithuania found only up to 13 cm across; dark blackish-brown, dark brown, bronze, matt. Tubes greyish, up to 3 cm long. Stem up to 12 cm long and 5 cm thick, slightly paler than the cap, with a network. Flesh white, not changing colour when cut, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap dark brown with a bronze tinge, the stem paler. Tasty. Very rare. Equal in value to the Porcini. Grows in deciduous forests, likes calcareous oak woods. Protected.

buozinis-pistunis.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, likes spruce and pine communities
buozinis-pistunis.features: Fruiting bodies yellowish-brown, much smaller than those of the Pestle Club
desc: Fruiting bodies club-shaped, clavate, wrinkled, 3-8 cm tall, up to 1.3 cm thick at the top, 0.3-0.5 cm in the lower part, yellowish, orange-yellow, when old yellowish-grey. Flesh whitish, yellowish, soft, mild in taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies similar to those of the Pestle Club, only bluntly knobbly at the top, spores smaller. Grows singly or in groups in spruce and pine forests. Edible, of low value. Uncommon. A massive club fungus, but half the size and much more common than the Pestle Club.

cerpetasis-baltikas.habitat: Coniferous forests, mossy pine forests, forest edges, forest clearings
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized or large. Cap 5—10 (12) cm across, yellowish-brown, pinkish-brown, matt, fibrous or as if slightly roughened. Gills whitish, brownish-yellowish, cream, spotted brown, adnate. Stem 6-12x1.5-3 cm, firm, fibrous, whitish, whitish-brownish, the base tapered, thickened in the middle. Flesh white, slightly bitter in taste, with a faint smell. Characteristic features: young cap conical, old flattened, with a rough surface and a prominent blunt umbo, margins bent downwards, as if cracked. Grows in small groups in coniferous forests. Edible fresh or salted, well boiled, but not very tasty. Very common.

cerpetasis-zvynadyglis.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially sandy pine forests, lichen pine forests
cerpetasis-zvynadyglis.features: Fruiting bodies woody, brittle, more common in October
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-12 (20) cm across, the whole surface as if armoured - covered with brown, blackish-brown scales. Spines whitish, when old greyish-brown, up to 12 mm long, decurrent. Stem 3—8x1—2.5 cm, thickening towards the base, grey, brownish, with a smooth surface. Flesh whitish, brownish, firm, bitter. Characteristic features: massive fruiting bodies, sometimes growing up to 30 cm across, like molehills; the underside of the cap is spiny, shaggy like a hedgehog's fur. Grows in groups, sometimes very close to one another. Edible when young. Very common, a striking fungal feature of lichen pine forests in late autumn.

cesnakinis-mazunis.features: Very tough, cap pinkish-brown, stem shiny, reddish-blackish
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap grows 1-3 cm across, matt, slightly wrinkled, yellowish-brownish, pale brownish-brown, thin, not fleshy. Gills distant, yellowish, cream. Stem round, 1-3 cm thick and up to 7 cm long, shiny, tough, reddish-brown, almost black in the lower part. Flesh thin, tough, whitish, with a strong smell of garlic, especially when rubbed between the fingers. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies with a strong garlic smell and taste. Grows on roots, mossy stumps, snags, branches, on conifer needles, singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Used as a seasoning instead of garlic. Very common.

cinoberine-slakabude.habitat: Coniferous, deciduous and mixed forests, among mosses
cinoberine-slakabude.features: Cap granular, gills whitish, stem roughened, with a ring
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-6 cm across, rarely larger, finely granular, yellowish, orange-red, red-lead coloured. Gills yellowish-white. Stem 4-8x0.4-1 cm, with a ring, below it the colour of the cap, granular, scaly, near the gills only dotted white. Flesh thin, yellowish, brownish, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap and stem granular, rough, yellowish orange-red. Grows singly, rarely in small groups. Edible, but of low value; some mycologists state that it is inedible. Very common.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-7 (10) cm across, when young convex-depressed, later goblet-shaped, finely fibrous, yellowish, greyish-yellowish, pale pinkish-brown. Gills white, later yellowish, crowded, decurrent. Stem 3-8x0.3-0.8 (1) cm, yellowish, brownish, with white fibrils. Flesh white, mild in taste, with a pleasant smell. Characteristic features: cap thin-fleshed, depressed, with a small umbo, not grooved. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together, in small groups; likes grassy places. Edible, very common. Especially good for flavouring soups.

dekandolio-trapiabude.habitat: Forests, parks, raised bogs, grassy, damp places
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 5-7 cm across, fibrous, matt, yellowish, cream, whitish or even white, thin-fleshed. Young gills white, quickly becoming brownish, brownish-brown, chocolate. Stem 5-8x0.3-0.5 cm, white, cream, brownish. Flesh white, not bitter, without a particular smell. Characteristic features: cap and stem yellowish, cream-coloured, very brittle. Grows in damp, wet grassy places and among nettles, on the ground, on rotten twigs or leaves, in groups. Edible, of low value, very common. Collecting is not recommended.

demetasis-baravykas.habitat: Mixed forests with oak, hornbeam, spruce, linden
demetasis-baravykas.features: Cap yellowish-greenish velvety, stem dotted with red
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap 8-20 cm across, greenish-yellowish-brown, greyish-greenish-brown, blackish velvety. Tubes up to 2.5 cm long, yellow; pores reddish-brown, turning blue instantly when pressed. Stem up to 15 cm long and 4-5 cm thick. Flesh yellow, turning blue instantly when cut, fading to bluish after a while, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: similar to the Lurid Bolete, but the stem of the Scarletina Bolete is dotted, without a network; likes the company of oaks and spruces. Grows singly or in small groups. Likes acidic soil. Edible. Protected. Uncommon.

didysis-kuokas.features: Hymenophore veined, folded and net-like, violet in colour
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy, 3-9 cm tall, shaped like an irregular blunt funnel or a rolled ear, when young purplish-violet, later pinkish-brownish, greyish-yellowish, greenish-yellowish; hymenophore veined and folded, net-like, greyish-violet, yellowish-violet. Stem short, tapering towards the base. Flesh whitish, soft, pleasant in taste, not bitter. Grows in mixed forests, likes calcareous soil. A good edible mushroom, but it must not be collected. Very rare, only two sites are known, in the Vilnius and Pakruojis districts. Endangered, protected.

didzioji-langermanija.habitat: Pastures, fallow land, scrub edges, forest edges, parks, gardens
didzioji-langermanija.features: Irregularly round, white, sometimes very large fruiting bodies
desc: Fruiting bodies very large, 10—20 (50) cm tall and up to 2 m in circumference, white, surface smooth, in old ones yellowish-brown, cracked into small patches. There is no stem. Flesh white, brown when old. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible when young. Not rare. In Lithuania specimens weighing from 3 to 15 kg have been found. This giant produces a huge number of spores - up to 7 trillion. If each spore grew into one such mushroom, within 2—3 years the Earth's surface would be covered with a layer 1 m thick. Medical scientists have also become interested in this mushroom.

didzioji-meskabude.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, among grasses
didzioji-meskabude.features: Mushrooms large, massive, with depressed caps, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies very large, robust. Cap grows up to 25 cm across (even 45 cm has been recorded), matt, fibrous, depressed, fleshy, white, cream, radially zoned, wrinkled. Gills very narrow, crowded, subdecurrent. Stem very short, 5-9 (10)x2-4 cm, white, when old brownish. Flesh thick, white, slightly bitter, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: white fruiting bodies, sometimes growing in rings even several dozen metres in diameter.

Grows among grasses, in humus-rich soil, in forests. Edible. An antibiotic that destroys tuberculosis bacilli has been isolated from it. Rare. The White Funnel (L. candidus) is very similar, but its fruiting bodies are smaller and it grows in coniferous forests. Protected.

dirvinis-pievagrybis.habitat: Pastures, meadows, farmsteads, fallow land, parks, gardens, rarely forests
dirvinis-pievagrybis.features: A white, yellowing mushroom of fertile soil, stem with a ring, without a volva
desc: Fruiting bodies large, fleshy. Cap 7—15 (20) cm across, finely fibrous, scaly, white, creamy white. Young gills greyish, quickly becoming pink, eventually blackish-brown. Stem 7-15 (20)x 1-3 cm, with a white ring, white, when old yellowish. Flesh fleshy, white, not changing colour when cut or turning slightly yellowish, with an aniseed smell and a pleasant taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies white, pleasant in taste, with an aniseed smell; gills pink, later chocolate, when old blackish-brown. Grows singly or in groups, likes humus-rich, fertile soil. A valuable edible mushroom, cultivated artificially. Sometimes grows large - even up to 1.5 kg in weight. Common.

drebuline-gelsvuole.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, especially damp, grassy, mossy ones
drebuline-gelsvuole.features: Fruiting bodies small, elastic, ochre-yellow in colour
desc: Fruiting bodies tiny. Cap 1-2 cm across, irregularly lobed-convex, yellowish, greenish-yellow, slimy, the underside dry. Stem 2—6x0.2—0.5 cm, cylindrical, granular, rough; the inside of an old stem is gelatinous, the colour of the cap, sometimes orange, golden yellow. Flesh thin, gelatinous, yellowish-whitish, with a mouldy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: spores with several transverse septa. Grows singly or in small groups in damp, grassy forests; likes oak, hornbeam and spruce communities. Edible, but of low value.

drebutinis-netikradyglis.habitat: Rotten stumps, windfalls, mostly of coniferous trees
drebutinis-netikradyglis.features: Fruiting body semicircular, shell-shaped, underside spiny
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap semicircular, fan-, shell- or tongue-shaped, up to 7 cm across, of jelly-like consistency, elastic, hard when dried, white, grey, violet-brown, sometimes dark brown; the upper side granular-warty, fibrous, velvety, the underside spiny (spines up to 3 mm long), whitish, bluish, most often greyish-bluish. Flesh thick, gelatinous, hard when dried. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together. Edible, used in salads, of low value, very watery.

dvispalve-lakabude.habitat: Pine forests (dry), parks, forest edges, copses, roadsides
dvispalve-lakabude.features: Gills, sometimes the cap and stem, with a violet tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1—4 (6) cm across, convex-flattened, broadly and shallowly depressed in the centre, matt, fibrous, finely scaly, brown, cinnamon-coloured, violet-pinkish-brown, fading with age. Gills thick, distant, broad, pale greyish-pink with a violet tinge, subdecurrent. Stem 3—8 (10)x0.3—0.8 cm, longitudinally violet-fibrous, greyish-pink, pinkish-brown, tough. Flesh greyish, brownish, not bitter, with a mushroomy smell. Characteristic features: as for mushrooms of the deceiver family — fruiting bodies fairly robust, gills violet. Grows singly or in small groups. Not rare. Edible, worth attention, especially good for flavouring soups.

dviziedis-pievagrybis.habitat: Squares, parks, gardens, less often (deciduous) forests
dviziedis-pievagrybis.features: Stem with a double ring, fruiting bodies greyish, yellowish, brownish
desc: Cap 5—10 (15) cm across, fleshy, hemispherical, later flattened, sometimes depressed in the centre, finely scaly, white, greyish-white, when old ochre-brown. Gills pale pink, when old purplish-black. Stem 4-7x2-4 cm, sometimes thickened in the middle, tapering at the base, with a double white ring. Flesh whitish, slowly turning pinkish when cut, up to 2.5 cm thick, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: most often grows along fences, in squares and parks; it is able to push its way through cracked asphalt or concrete. Grows singly or in small groups. It is not advisable to collect it near busy streets, in squares or along fences, because the mushrooms may have accumulated car exhaust pollutants.

dvokiancioji-umede.features: Robust slimy fruiting bodies, a repulsive smell
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 7-15 (18) cm across, slimy, shiny, margins bent downwards, the cuticle peels well, yellowish-brown, dirty ochre, rusty-bronze in colour. Gills cream, the edges with droplets of colourless liquid, as if dewy, adnate. Stem 5-12x2-4 cm, whitish, greyish. Characteristic features: the Almond Brittlegill (R. laurocerasi) is similar; it differs in its smaller fruiting bodies and a distinct smell of almonds. Protected. Grows in groups, especially in birch and oak woods. Edible, but not valued because of its bitter taste and unpleasant smell. Uncommon in recent years.

dydysis-pievagrybis.habitat: Coniferous forests, most often old spruce stands
dydysis-pievagrybis.features: Massive fruiting bodies, grows only in forests, stem long, thick
desc: Cap 5-15 (20) cm across, fleshy, at first bell-shaped, later flattened, slightly depressed, the central part coffee-coloured, the margins greyish-brown, brownish Young gills pink, when old pinkish-red, dirty purplish-brown, broad. Stem massive, 8-15 (25)x 1.5-3 cm, of uniform thickness, brownish, brown, fibrous, with a large ring with brown scales. Flesh fleshy, white, turning red instantly when cut, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: the surface of the cap and stem, like the flesh, turns red instantly when pressed, cut or broken. Grows in small groups, in groups, rarely singly. A good edible mushroom. Uncommon.

dygliuotasis-pumpotaukslis.habitat: Damp deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests
desc: Fruiting bodies 3-5 cm across, globular, broadly pear-shaped, beautifully yellowish-brown, when old brown, spiny (spines up to 7 mm long), shaggy (resembling a hedgehog). Flesh white when young, when old greyish-brown, chocolate-brown. Grows singly in forests. An uncommon, beautiful mushroom. The Dusky Puffball (L. umbrinus) is very similar, only its fruiting bodies are covered with spiny warts which almost all crumble and fall off, leaving the surface of the fruiting body rough but not hairy.

eglyninine-rudmese.habitat: Spruce forests, mixed spruce forests, especially with oak
eglyninine-rudmese.features: Similar to a larger Saffron Milkcap, but grows only in spruce forests
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, flattened, margins incurved, with greenish spots, pinkish-orange, dirty ochre in colour. Gills orange-ochre, brownish-red, exuding orange milk when broken or cut, adnate, subdecurrent. Stem 3-7x1-2.5 cm, orange-brownish. Flesh fairly thick, firm, carrot-, orange-cream-coloured, exuding orange milk when cut or broken, which later turns green. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies pinkish-orange, smaller than those of the Saffron Milkcap. Grows singly, in small groups, in groups. Its food value is the same as that of the Saffron Milkcap; mushroom pickers probably do not even distinguish them as separate species. Fairly common.

eglyninis-piengrybis.features: Cap smoky brown, velvety, milk white
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, domed, later becoming flattened, depressed, with an umbo, velvety, blackish-brown, blackish ochre-brown, when old fading to a paler brownish-grey colour. Young gills pale ochre, later yellowish-brown, crowded, adnate. Stem 3—7x1—2.5 cm, the colour of the cap, paler near the gills, with white mould-like down at the base. Flesh whitish, slowly turning red when pressed or cut; the white milk and the flesh turn reddish on reacting with air. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies blackish ochre-brown, turning red when cut. Grows a few fruiting bodies together in old, damp, thinned-out spruce forests with pine. Very rare. Edible, but of low value. Should be classed as worthy of protection.

elnine-skydabude.habitat: On deciduous, rarely coniferous stumps, snags, windfalls
elnine-skydabude.features: Grows only on rotting wood, gills pinkish-brownish
desc: Cap 5-12 (15) cm across, when young conical, later flattened, thin-fleshed, fragile, fibrous, slimy and shiny in damp weather, brown, greyish-brown, yellowish-brown, even blackish-brown. Gills white, later pink, pinkish-rose, pinkish, free. Stem 5-12 (15)x0.5-2 cm, thickening towards the base, greyish, brownish, with greyish-black fibrils. Flesh white, mild in taste, with an unpleasant smell. Characteristic features: cap from yellowish-brown to blackish-brown. Grows singly, less often a few fruiting bodies together. Edible. Common. The Black-edged Shield (P. atromarginatus) is similar, only its fruiting bodies are blacker and the gill edges are dotted black. Grows in the same places.

fechtnerio-baravykas-.habitat: Grassy, calcareous, open, light oak woods
fechtnerio-baravykas-.features: Young fruiting bodies yellow, yellowish, stem reddish-pink in the middle
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-12 (15-20) cm across, fleshy, matt, yellowish-grey, grey, brownish-grey, turning brown when pressed. Tubes at first yellowish, later golden yellow, turning blue when pressed. Stem 8-12x2—5 cm, yellow, later yellowish-grey, reddish-pink in the middle, the network weakly developed. Flesh yellowish, yellow, turning blue when broken, eventually fading to a dirty yellowish colour, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: tubes yellow, flesh yellow, turning blue when cut; grows only in grassy oak woods. Appears in small groups. Edible. Warmth-loving, grows in warm, humid summers. Rare, protected.

garbanotoji-alvyte.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forests, forest clearings, scrub, roadsides
garbanotoji-alvyte.features: Cap lobed, stem longitudinally pitted and ribbed
desc: Fruiting bodies small, medium-sized. Cap 2-3 (4) cm across, saddle-shaped, made of several irregularly folded lobes, whitish, yellowish. Stem 3-7 (8) x 1-2.5 cm, white, longitudinally ribbed, deeply grooved, hollow. Flesh white, thin, brittle, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap and stem fairly brittle, almost white in colour, grows mostly in autumn. Appears singly or in groups. Edible fresh or dried. Common. An easily remembered, recognisable mushroom.

gauruotasis-meslagrybis.habitat: Fields, pastures, squares, parks, fallow land, forest roadsides, clearings
gauruotasis-meslagrybis.features: Cap shaggy, stem with a ring, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 6-15 (18) cm tall and 2-4 cm wide, when young elongated conical, cylindrical, when old bell-shaped conical; the surface at first smooth, later cracked, breaking up into large, recurved scales. Young gills white, old ones brownish-black, black, crowded, fragile, soft, free; when old they liquefy and drip off in thick drops. Stem 8-20 (30)x2-4 cm, cylindrical, slightly thickening towards the base, white, finely fibrous, with a white movable ring. Flesh white, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: white, shaggy mushrooms growing in open places. Grows in groups, colonies or singly, in fertile places. Very common. Eaten young; tasty, especially fresh with a sour cream sauce. In some countries it is cultivated to make mushroom juice.

gauruotkotis-nuosedis.features: Similar to the robust webcap, only the young gills of this one are cream
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 7-12 (15) cm across, bell-shaped, eventually flattened, slimy, shiny, matt when dry, ochre-yellow, the margins encircled by a band of white veil; in young caps the shaggy, downy veil is joined to the stem. Gills cream, without a violet tinge, when old blackish-brown, adnate. Stem 5-12x1.5-2.5 cm, firm, white, with white zigzag shaggy bands. Flesh white, thick, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap margins and stem with a white shaggy veil; grows only under pines and spruces. Appears in small groups. Edible, uncommon.

gelsvarude-musmire.habitat: Coniferous and deciduous forests, also boggy places
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-10 cm across, sometimes larger, surface smooth, rarely with remnants of the yellow veil, slimy, shiny, pale yellowish-brown, orange-brown, margins grooved. Gills white, later yellowish, free. Stem 7-16x0.5-1.5 cm, white, without a ring, at the base with a loose whitish, brownish volva. Flesh white, soft, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: stem without a ring, white, long, gradually thickening towards the base. Grows singly or in small groups, quite often in boggy pine forests, among sphagnum mosses. Edible, but collecting is not recommended, because it can be confused with the poisonous Common Amanita (paprastoji musmirė). Common.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 3-8 (13) cm across, but larger ones are also found, yellow, with greenish, brown or blackish scales. Gills yellow, crowded, adnate. Stem yellow, up to 8 cm long and 1.3 cm thick. Flesh firm, yellow, with an unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Characteristic features: cap scaly. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together on fallen spruces or pines, rarely on their snags or stumps. Edible, but of low value.

gelsvejantysis-baltikas.features: Cap, gills and stem turning yellowish
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-5 (7) cm across, when young conical, later flattened, with an umbo, not fleshy, finely fibrous-scaly, grey, brownish-grey; in old ones the margins are yellowish. Gills whitish, adnexed, adnate. Stem 2-5x0.3-1 cm, fragile, white, later grey, brownish, turning yellowish. Flesh thin, greyish, pleasant in taste, with a faint mealy smell. Characteristic features: similar to the Grey Knight and other grey-coloured knights, only its fruiting bodies are more delicate and turn yellowish. Grows in groups, under birches and pines, likes open places. Edible, tasty.

gelsvoji-stirnabude.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, likes mossy places
gelsvoji-stirnabude.features: Differs from the Tawny Funnel in its yellow, spotted caps
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 4-8 (10) cm across, flattened, depressed, sometimes with a small umbo, ochre, pinkish-yellow, yellow, the surface with watery spots. Gills narrow, crowded, yellowish, decurrent. Stem 3-6x0.5-1.5 cm, the colour of the cap, thickening towards the base. Flesh thin, tough, yellowish. Characteristic features: the cap surface has faint square or round water-soaked spots. Grows in small groups, mostly in coniferous forests. Common.

gelsvoji-voveraite.habitat: Grassy, damp deciduous and coniferous forests, especially mixed spruce forests
desc: Fruiting bodies not fleshy, small. Cap 3—6 cm across, also grows larger, shaped like a deep funnel, matt, fibrous, with irregularly lobed, wavy, crimped margins, ochre-brown, yellowish-blackish-brown. There are no gills, only a network of thickened, dichotomously branched orange-yellow ridges. Stem 3-4x0.3-1 cm, tube-shaped, tapering downwards, orange, golden yellow. Flesh thin, yellowish, pleasant in taste, with a strong fruity smell. Characteristic features: cap dirty yellowish, dark yellowish-brown. Sometimes grows in large groups in forests, in damp, grassy places. Edible, but of no special value. Not rare.

geltonasis-kazlekas.habitat: Pine forests, sometimes even boggy ones, higher-lying places
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 3-12 (13) cm across, fibrous, fibrous-granular, slimy in damp weather, yellowish-grey, yellowish-brown, brownish-yellow. Tubes greyish-yellowish-greenish, in older ones greenish-yellow, dirty greyish-green, turning blue when pressed. Stem 4—8x2—3 cm, sturdy, smooth, orange-yellow, without a ring. Flesh yellow, turning blue when cut or broken, with a mild smell and taste. Characteristic features: greyish orange-yellow fruiting bodies, appearing in pine forests and forests with pine. Sometimes also called the pine-heath bolete. Grows in groups, less often singly, under pines. A tasty, valuable edible mushroom. Very common, loved by everyone.

geltonasis-piengrybis.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially damp, grassy spruce forests
geltonasis-piengrybis.features: Fruiting bodies slimy, cap and stem spotted
desc: Fruiting bodies large, robust. Cap grows up to 25 cm across, with concentric zones, fibrous, fleshy, slimy, chrome yellow, lemon yellow, yellowish-ochre. Gills whitish, later brownish-ochre, spotted brown, adnate, slightly decurrent. Stem 3—7x1.5—3.5 cm, yellow, slimy, spotted. Characteristic features: flesh yellowish, darkening when broken or cut, with a sharp, burning taste; the milk is white and quickly turns yellow on reacting with air. The largest milkcap of spruce forests. Grows in groups. Uncommon, edible; although listed in the Red Data Book of Lithuania, it may be collected, because it is widespread and abundant.

geltonkotis-skiautenelis.habitat: Wood of deciduous, rarely coniferous trees
geltonkotis-skiautenelis.features: Mostly a saprotroph of deciduous trees, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-10 cm across, sometimes larger, fleshy, elastic, yellowish-green, bluish-green on a yellow background, velvety, felty, margins bent downwards. Gills crowded, adnate, yellow, ochre. Stem short, thick, 1-2x2 cm, with brownish scales, dotted, hairy, yellow. Flesh spongy, himpri, pale, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fleshy, greenish-yellow fruiting bodies, elastic, irregularly shell-shaped, the gill edge notched. Grows a few fruiting bodies together. Common. Edible, of low value, not recommended for eating.

geltonoji-skiauteryte.habitat: Forests, forest margins, among grasses and mosses
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 (6) cm tall and 1-2 cm wide, shaped like a spatula or a tennis racket, folded and wrinkled, soft yellow, orange-yellow. Stem 3—5 cm long and 2.5 cm thick, white, broadly enclosed by the cap. Flesh soft. Characteristic features: spores very large, with transverse septa. Grows singly, but sometimes in groups, next to one another, several dozen fruiting bodies, in forests. Rare. Edible, but of low value; it is left untouched.

geltonporis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Oak woods, mixed forests with oak and hazel
geltonporis-raudonvirsis.features: Flesh yellow, turning pinkish when cut, later blackening
desc: Fruiting bodies not robust. Cap 5-10 cm across, rarely larger (12-15 cm), mostly domed, only when old flat, dry, matt, greenish-yellowish-brown, orange-yellow with a brown tinge, yellowish-fibrous. Tubes 1—2 (3) cm long, greyish-yellow; pores yellowish, lemon yellow, in old mushrooms greenish-brownish, violet-brown when pressed. Flesh lemon yellow, turning pinkish when cut or broken and later darkening to black, not bitter. Characteristic features: tubes lemon yellow, turning pinkish when pressed or cut, eventually blackening; likes the company of oak. Grows singly, under oaks and hazels. Rare, edible.

geltonrudis-baltikas.habitat: Deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, damper places - under birches
geltonrudis-baltikas.features: Cap reddish-brown, gills yellow, spotted pinkish
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, yellowish-brown, the margins radially lobed. Gills yellowish, in older mushrooms brownish-yellow with brownish-brown spots, adnate. Stem 5-10 (12)x1-2 cm in size, yellowish. Flesh thin, yellow, not bitter, with a smell of cucumber. Characteristic features: grows only under birches, cap margins lobed, crimped. Appears singly and in groups around Ukmergė and in some other places in central Lithuania; also wrongly called guotė (milkcap); popular. Tasty salted or fresh, eaten well boiled. Common.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-12 cm across, irregularly flattened, slightly depressed in the middle, matt, greenish-yellow, golden yellow, brownish-yellow, lemon-coloured, the margins paler. Young gills yellowish-white, later ochre, adnexed. Stem 5—8x1—3 cm, white, turning greyish with age. Flesh white, turning greyish with age, not bitter or slightly acrid, firm. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies turn greyish with age. Grows in small groups. Edible, tasty. Common. The Geranium Brittlegill (R. fellea) is similar, but it grows mostly in deciduous forests and is much paler in colour.

girinis-pievagrybis.features: Differs from the Horse Mushroom in smaller spores and habitat
desc: Cap 5-10 cm across, convex-flattened, sometimes depressed in the centre, not fleshy, white, greyish-white, fibrous, scaly. Gills pinkish, later purplish-brown, eventually blackish-brown. Stem 6-8 (10)x1-2 cm, thickened at the base, whitish, brownish, with a hanging ring. Flesh thin, whitish, aromatic. Characteristic features: grows only in forests and parks, fruiting bodies greyish-white. Grows singly, sometimes a few fruiting bodies together. A tasty edible mushroom. Common. The poisonous Yellow Stainer (Agaricus xanthodermd) is very similar to the Horse Mushroom, the Field Mushroom and the Wood Mushroom; however, this mushroom occurs rarely, its fruiting bodies have an unpleasant carbolic (phenol) smell, and when cut they instantly turn bright yellow.

Fruiting bodies small, medium-sized. Cap 3-8 cm across, thin-fleshed, pale ash-coloured, grey, brownish-grey, fading, matt, fibrous. Gills whitish, later yellowish-brownish, crowded, adnate. Stem 3—5x0.5-1.5 cm, whitish, when old brownish. Flesh thin, greyish, brittle, without a particular smell or taste. The milk is white, scanty. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies brittle, delicate, grey; the milk does not change colour. Grows singly, most often in groups. Edible, very common. The Coconut Milkcap (.L. glyciosmus(Fr.: Fr. Fr.)) is very similar; it differs in its smaller, acrid fruiting bodies with an insistently pleasant smell. Rarer, also grows under birches. Edible. Of low value.

gleivetasis-nuosedis.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially dry pine forests
gleivetasis-nuosedis.features: Stem white, cap chestnut-coloured, slimy, spores large
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, fleshy. Cap 5-8 cm across, also grows larger, very slimy, shiny, yellowish-brown, orange, reddish-brown, the centre darker. Gills greyish, when old reddish-brown, adnate. Stem 7-12x0.5-2 (3) cm, white, slimy. Flesh yellowish, not bitter, thick. Characteristic features: stem with a white, grey, slimy coating of a cobweb-like veil. Grows most often in small groups. Edible, very common. The Blue-stemmed (Cortinarius collinitus) and Slimy Webcaps are very similar and even grow in similar places, but the stem of the Slimy Webcap is always white, without a bluish or violet coating.

glicioji-geltonpede.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially mossy spruce forests
glicioji-geltonpede.features: Stem tapering at the base, bright yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 (12) cm across, very slimy, greyish-brown, brownish-violet, when old with black spots. Young gills are greyish, old ones spotted black, almost black, distant, thick, forked. Stem 3—9x1—2.3 cm in size, greyish, greyish-brownish, beautifully yellow at the base, near the gills with a ring zone, quite slimy. Characteristic features: cap and stem very slimy, flesh fairly thick, soft, white, pleasant in taste. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together, mostly in spruce forests. Edible, pleasant in taste, only it turns black when boiled. Not rare. Adding a little citric acid when boiling - it will blacken less.

glitusis-piengrybis.features: Cap not zoned, flesh white, blackish-violet when cut
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, slimy, not zoned (rarely one or two faint zones only near the margins), flattened, slightly depressed, yellowish greyish-brownish. Gills white, quickly turning yellowish, crowded, subdecurrent, when old spotted violet. Stem 5-10x0.5-2 cm, slimy, yellowish, brownish. Flesh white, not bitter, quickly stained violet when cut or broken. The milk is white, soon turning violet when exuded. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies slimy; the milk is white and, once exuded, like the flesh, quickly stains violet, blackish-violet. Grows singly or in small groups in deciduous and mixed, less often coniferous forests; likes the company of birch and goat willow. Edible. Of low value. Very rare.

gluosnine-kreivabude.habitat: Forests, parks, roadsides, farmsteads, on dead, less often living deciduous trees
gluosnine-kreivabude.season: Summer, especially autumn, even spring, mild winter
gluosnine-kreivabude.features: Blackish-grey cap, stem white, lateral or eccentric
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, large. Cap 5-12 (15) cm across, fan-shaped, semicircular, when old flattened, fleshy, surface smooth, ash-grey, slate-grey, grey, yellowish-grey, blackish-grey, with a violet tinge. Gills white, when old yellowish-grey, broad, pinkish, running far down the stem (long decurrent), the edges not toothed. Stem 1-5x0.5-2.5 cm, eccentric or lateral, firm, white, yellowish, yellowish-brownish, fibrous. Flesh fairly thick, white, soft, juicy, not bitter, with a mealy smell. Characteristic features: fan-shaped fruiting bodies, gills not toothed. Grows singly, in small groups, in colonies. A valuable edible mushroom, cultivated artificially in many countries (including Lithuania). Of interest to medical scientists.

grakscioji-zvynabude.features: Cap with white scales, stem smooth
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 7-8 (10) cm across, white, yellowish, scaly. Gills white, when old brownish, with a soft pink tinge. Stem 7-12 (15)x1-1.5 cm, white, when old brownish, with a white ring. Flesh white, with an unpleasant smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies white, cap scaly, gills turning brownish when pressed. Grows several or even a dozen or more fruiting bodies together. In September 2004, in the Dubrava forests, Šilėnai forest district (compartment 66, sub-compartment 14), in a planted spruce stand (50-60 years old), hundreds of fruiting bodies grew in every row of spruces, under every tree. Perhaps this was influenced by the huge spruces whose branches had not yet interlocked. This was more likely some kind of anomaly, since the fruiting bodies were also considerably smaller. Edible, but of low value.

grakstusis-kazlekas.habitat: Parks, squares, forests, only under larches
desc: Fruiting bodies large, beautiful. Cap grows up to 10 cm across, yellowish-brown, orange-yellow or reddish-brown in colour, slimy. Tubes yellow. Stem the colour of the cap, with a yellow ring. Flesh yellow, soft, with a mild smell and taste, not changing colour. Characteristic features: stem with a yellow ring, flesh not changing colour when cut. Grows singly or in small groups, only under larches. Edible, excellent, not rare. Medical scientists are interested in the properties of this mushroom.

grudetoji-slakabude.features: Cap coarsely granular, spores small, non-amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 (6) cm across, flattened, with an umbo, granular, wrinkled in the middle, finely scaly, orange-brown, brownish-red; the margins with a ragged fringe of the partial veil. Gills narrow, crowded, white, later yellowish, adnate. Stem 4-8x0.3-0.8 cm, with a ring, paler above it, only dotted, and below the ring fibrous, scaly, brownish-pink. Flesh yellowish, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies reddish-brown, redder than those of the Vermilion Powdercap. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together, among mosses. Edible, but of low value; some mycologists state that it is inedible.

gubriuotoji-samanbude.features: Cap flatly depressed, with a small umbo, spores amyloid
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.5-3 cm across, matt, fibrous, sometimes concentrically zoned, violet-grey, blackish-grey or even greyish-brown. Gills white, very crowded, narrow, spotted pinkish, decurrent. Stem 3-9x0.3—0.7 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh thin, whitish, spotted pinkish, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap and stem steel-grey, gills cream, white when young. Grows in autumn until the snow, singly or in small groups. Edible, of low value, but very common; good for flavouring soups.

gumbuotasis-baltnuosedis.habitat: Coniferous and mixed forests, especially pine forests
gumbuotasis-baltnuosedis.features: Similar to the webcaps, but the spores are colourless, smooth-walled
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 cm across, also grows larger. When young it is hemispherical, later convex-flattened, with a blunt umbo, yellowish-brown, greyish-brown, brownish, the margins paler, with remnants of the white veil. Gills white, later brownish-yellowish, adnate. Stem 5-10x1-2 cm, white, brown-fibrous, bulbous at the base, up to 3 cm across. Flesh white, soft, thick, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap yellowish, gills whitish, stem bulbous. Grows singly. Edible, uncommon.

gyslotasis-ploksciagrybis.features: Cap surface ridged and wrinkled, flesh smelling of chlorine
desc: Fruiting bodies 3-12 (13) cm across, shaped like a broad-bottomed, irregular dish with spreading margins, the surface veined and ridged, wrinkled, yellowish-brown, pinkish-brown, dark brown. Hymenium pale greyish-brown, brown. Stem short, up to 1 cm, merging into the cap, whitish pale brown. Flesh white, soft, with a smell of chlorine that disappears on boiling. Characteristic features: cap large, shaped like an irregular dish. Grows singly or in small groups in coniferous and deciduous forests and parks; likes sandy, humus-rich, damp soil, even rotten wood. Fairly rare, edible.

ilgasis-kukurdvelkis.habitat: Deciduous and coniferous forests, pastures, parks, fallow land
ilgasis-kukurdvelkis.features: White, spiny, warty, pestle-shaped fruiting bodies
desc: Fruiting bodies 7-15 (20) x3—10 cm in size, consisting of a thick cylindrical stem and a globular head. They resemble a pestle; when young they are white, later yellowish-brownish, brownish. Surface granular, with pointed warts. Flesh soft, cottony, with a pleasant taste and smell. Characteristic features: head round, with crimped folds near the stem. Grows singly or in small groups, in summer and autumn, in forests, parks and fallow land. Common. Edible when young. Sometimes cup-shaped remains of the stem are still found in spring.

invalo-sakocius.habitat: On fallen, rotting conifer needles, especially under spruces
invalo-sakocius.features: Fruiting bodies yellowish-brown, tips sharply branched
desc: Fruiting bodies shaped like a small bush, coral or shrub, 3-8 cm tall, dichotomously or irregularly branched, ochre, yellowish-ochre, when old ochre-brown in colour. Going upwards the bush widens, the branches divide, become denser, thinner and more pointed, and are sharply branched at the tips. Stem short, paler than the branches. Flesh white, later yellowish, with an unpleasant smell and bitter taste. Grows in groups or even colonies on spruce needles in forests, especially spruce forests, and also in mixed forests. Young mushrooms are edible. Very common. The Greening Coral (R. ochraceo-virens) is very similar, only it differs in its greenish-ochre fruiting bodies with a violet tinge. Edible

juodkote-ugniabude.habitat: Forests, parks, gardens, roadsides, living and dying deciduous trees
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-10 cm across, when young domed, later flattened, with an umbo, smooth, slimy, chestnut-coloured, yellowish-brown, orange-brown, fading to yellow, yellowish. Gills crowded, fairly thick, white, yellowish, adnate. Stem 3-10x0.3-1.3 cm, cartilaginous, sometimes twisted, yellowish, yellowish-brownish near the gills, blackish-brown lower down, velvety. Flesh soft, yellowish, pleasant in taste, without a particular smell. Characteristic features: cap slimy, with a smooth surface, stem velvety. Grows in autumn, even in mild winters (when the air temperature is +5 °C), in small groups, on damaged parts of deciduous trees and shrubs. Edible, cultivated artificially in some countries. Very common.

juodmese-umede.habitat: Coniferous, rarely deciduous forests, likes the shelter of pines
juodmese-umede.features: Gills thin, crowded, greyish, flesh turning brownish, later blackish
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 7-12 (18) cm across, fleshy, the cuticle does not peel; damp, slimy, matt; when young it is white, quickly becoming cream, eventually greyish-blackish, dirty black. Gills cream, when old greyish-blackish, thin, crowded, subdecurrent. Stem 3-6 (10)x2-5 cm, firm, white, greyish, later the colour of the cap. Flesh not bitter in taste, turning greyish or only slightly brownish when cut or broken, later blackish. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies massive, darkening while still emerging from the moss, very often maggoty. Grows most often in groups in dry pine forests. Edible, very common.

juosvadryze-sydabude.habitat: Parks, greenhouses, gardens on old manure, at the edges of compost heaps
juosvadryze-sydabude.features: Cap greyish-blackish fibrous, gills pink, stem white
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 (10) cm across, when young bell-shaped, later convex-flattened, greyish-brown, greenish-blackish, blackish-grey; an old cap fades to greyish, streaked. Gills at first white, later pinkish-rose. Stem 5-10x0.5-1.5 cm, slightly thickening towards the base, white, without a ring, the base enclosed by a lobed, greyish-brownish, greenish-brown volva. Flesh white, thick, soft, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: cap greyish-blackish, stem without a ring, but with a prominent, large volva. Grows in groups. Edible. Rare. Warmth-loving. Widespread in warm-climate regions. In India and China it is cultivated in special premises, as field mushrooms and oyster mushrooms are here.

juosvarude-guote.features: Cap convex, irregularly flat, with an umbo, blackish-brown
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap grows up to 10 cm across and larger, fleshy, surface matt, fibrous, greyish-brown, blackish greyish-brown. Gills brownish, thick, grey, greyish-cream, slightly decurrent. Stem up to 10-12 cm long and 2-2.5 cm thick, slightly paler than the cap. Flesh white, thick, soft, without a particular smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: the largest mushroom of the woodwax genus. Grows among mosses in old-growth forests, sometimes in large groups (in the Viešvilė Reserve in 2000 two sites were found where 23 and 33 fruiting bodies grew). Edible. Protected.

juosvasis-piengrybis.habitat: Forests, parks, especially grassy, damp spruce forests
juosvasis-piengrybis.features: Milk white, does not change colour
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-15 (20) cm across, sometimes even larger, massive, fleshy, flattened, depressed, margins incurved, surface rough, fibrous, slimy, yellowish-green, later blackish-green, greenish-brown. Gills crowded, narrow, white, quickly becoming cream, greyish-yellowish, with white milk. Stem 3—7x1—3 cm, fairly short, thick, the colour of the cap, with white milk. Flesh thick (up to 2 cm), yellowish, with abundant bitter, burning-tasting white milk. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies dirty greenish-brown in colour. Grows in groups, rarely singly; likes grassy, damp places and the company of spruce and birch. Very common, edible; after boiling in salted water the bitterness disappears.

juosvasis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Damp, grassy birch woods, mixed forests, pine forests with birch
juosvasis-raudonvirsis.features: Cap blackish, surface felt-like, stem with black fibrils
desc: Cap 5—15 cm across, round, eventually convex-horizontal, softly velvety, felt-like, blackish-brown, dirty greyish-blackish, fleshy. Tubes white, when old greyish-cream in colour. Stem 7—10 (13)x1—4 cm, coarsely black-fibrous, thickening towards the base. Flesh white, yellowish under the cuticle, thick, firm, not changing colour when cut. Characteristic features: massive, gloomy-looking, blackish fruiting bodies. Edible. Grows in deciduous and mixed forests, under birches, singly or in small groups. Rare.

juosvazalis-baltikas.habitat: Coniferous forests, mostly pine forests with birch
desc: Medium-sized mushrooms. Cap 3—6 (10) cm across, with a blunt umbo, shiny, slimy, radially streaked, bluish-grey, grey, sometimes with a bluish-violet tinge. Gills white, when old greenish-yellowish, adnate. Stem 6-10x1-3 cm in size, white, whitish-yellowish. Flesh greyish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap bluntly conical, in older mushrooms flattened but with an umbo; gills and stem yellowish, greenish-yellowish. Grows in groups. Tasty fresh, salted, dried, pickled; in value it is not inferior to the Yellow Knight. Very common. Quite similar to the Ashen Knight (Tricholoma virgatum), which is mildly poisonous; the mushroom picker should not forget this.

juosvazvynis-raudonvirsis.features: Stem covered with black scales. Cap more orange in colour
desc: Fruiting bodies robust, fleshy. Cap grows up to 20 cm across, fibrous, scaly, orange-yellow, yellowish-brown. Tubes up to 3 cm long, greyish; pores greyish. Stem 7-20x2-3 cm, white, already black-scaly when young. Characteristic features: grows only under birches; the flesh is white, when broken or cut it becomes violet-pink, purplish-brown, greenish-blue at the base of the stem. Appears in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, in larger or smaller groups, rarely singly. Edible, very valuable.

juosvoji-umede.features: Gills cream, distant, thick, turning red when pressed
desc: In the colour, shape and size of the fruiting body and in its habitat, Russula nigricans is very similar to Russula adusta; it differs in its distant, thick gills; when cut or broken, the cap, gills, flesh or stem, unlike those of R. adusta, instantly turn red, eventually becoming red, turning greyish and finally black. Flesh not bitter. Characteristic features: thicker, distant gills and smaller spores. Fruiting bodies are very often maggoty, especially the stem. Grows in summer and autumn, in small groups among mosses, more widespread in coniferous forests. Edible, not rare. Much loved by insects, most often maggoty.

kamparinis-piengrybis.features: Fruiting bodies, especially when dried, with a strong smell of camphor
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 cm across, convex, later flattened with a depressed centre, with a faint umbo, margins zoned (ridged), dirty greyish-pinkish-brown, reddish-brown, fading to brownish. Gills the colour of the cap, brownish-cream, crowded, subdecurrent. Stem 2-7 (8)x0.5-1 cm, fragile, the colour of the cap or slightly paler. Flesh thin, brownish, firm, with a strong smell of camphor, not bitter, with white, mild milk that does not change colour. Characteristic features: dirty brownish-red fruiting bodies, the milk white, not changing colour. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, of low value. Common. Suitable for use as a seasoning.

karcialakste-umede.features: Gills bitter, flesh not bitter, turning reddish when cut, later greyish
desc: Fruiting bodies of the colour and size of Russula adusta and Russula nigricans. Cap from the very beginning blackish-brown, dirty yellowish-greyish-brown, with a blackish tinge. Young gills white, later becoming cream, crowded, very bitter in taste, strongly decurrent. Stem white, later the colour of the cap. Flesh thick, firm, turning slightly reddish when broken or cut, then fading to grey, not bitter. Characteristic features: very similar to Russula adusta and Russula nigricans, but mostly widespread in deciduous forests. Grows singly or in small groups, likes humus-rich, loose soil. So far found only in the Bukta forests (Marijampolė district). Edible. Should be classed as protected.

karpotasis-pumpotaukslis.features: White fruiting bodies covered with dense, easily rubbed-off spines
desc: A mushroom very well known to everyone. Fruiting body 3—8 cm tall, the lower part tapering into a stem. White, when old brown, covered with easily rubbed-off, sharp warts and spines. Flesh white, with a pleasant smell and taste, turning brown when old. Characteristic features: similar to the Pestle Puffball, but smaller, and the stem is much shorter and tapered. Grows in forests, in groups on the ground, less often on rotten wood. Young ones, while the flesh is white, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste, are edible; when cooked they are yellowish in colour. Very common; of interest to medical scientists.

kartusis-pipirbaravykis.features: Small yellowish-brown fruiting bodies, flesh with a peppery taste
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 2-3 (3) cm across, convex-horizontal, matt, slightly fibrous, sticky only in damp weather, yellowish, yellowish-brown, brownish. Tubes reddish-yellow, brown, up to 1 cm long; pores red. Stem 3-7x0.3-1 cm, the colour of the cap, tapering towards the base. Flesh yellowish, greenish-yellow. Characteristic features: underside of the cap brownish-red, flesh with a sharp peppery taste. Grows singly and in small groups in pine, spruce and mixed forests. Edible, used as a seasoning instead of pepper. Common.

kazlekas.features: A slimy, yellowish-brown mushroom of sandy pine forests
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized, rarely large. Cap 3-8 (12) cm across, slimy, covered with an easily peeled cuticle, chocolate-brown, yellowish-brown, reddish-brown, yellow. Young tubes pale yellow, with droplets of white liquid, covered with a violet membrane; later, when the membrane disappears, they become greyish-yellow. Stem 3-10x1-3 cm, with a greyish-violet or yellowish-brownish ring. Flesh white, yellowish, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste, not changing colour when cut. Characteristic features: cap very slimy, stem with a ring, the colour of the flesh does not change. Grows in sandy, even grassy pine forests and spruce forests with pine, in groups, sometimes in colonies. The cuticle is peeled off. A tasty edible mushroom. Very common. Also of interest to medical scientists.

kele-umede.habitat: Spruce forests, pine forests, mixed forests
kele-umede.features: Cap and stem purplish-red, with a violet tinge
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-8 cm across, sometimes larger, flattened, the centre depressed, matt, rough, purplish-violet, reddish-brown, brownish-violet, the margins paler. Gills white, later yellowish, crowded, brittle, adnate. Stem 3-8x0.5—2 cm, of uniform thickness, with a purple, pinkish-bluish tinge. Flesh white, firm, with a pleasant smell and a bitter, acrid taste. Characteristic features: flesh very bitter in taste; most often grows in wood-sorrel pine forests. Appears in small groups or singly in damp forests, likes the company of spruce, less often pine. Edible when well boiled, but because of its bitter taste it is not recommended to collect it.

Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3—5 cm across, when young egg-shaped, later broadly conical, yellowish-brown, coffee-coloured in the middle with glistening granules that quickly disappear, crimped and grooved. Gills greyish, quickly becoming greyish-brownish, black when old. Stem 3-8x0.3-0.6 cm, white, the base yellowish, fibrous. Flesh thin, yellowish, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: yellow, brown fruiting bodies. Grows in groups, colonies, on rotting wood, snags, stumps, windfalls, sometimes even on the roots of living trees. Very common. Edible when young, of low value. Poisoning is possible if it is consumed with alcoholic drinks. Of interest to medical scientists.

kietasis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Deciduous forests, under aspens and poplars
kietasis-raudonvirsis.features: Flesh white, firm, turning reddish when cut, turning green at the stem base
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-12 (15) cm across, matt, fibrous, greyish-brown, dirty greyish, yellowish-brown, blackish-brown, sometimes uneven, cracked. Tubes greyish, eventually greyish-cream, up to 3 cm long. Pores greenish-brownish. Stem 5-15x1-3.5 cm, firm, white, longitudinally blackish-fibrous, rough, spotted green at the base. Flesh white, turning reddish when cut, later becoming violet-pinkish, bluish-green at the base of the stem. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies firm, the surface of the cap and especially of the stem rough.
Grows singly or in small groups in deciduous forests, likes lighter habitats. Edible, rare.

kietoji-dirvabude.features: Fruiting bodies yellowish, yellowish-brown, fading, grows in open places
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3—6 cm across, sometimes larger, flattened, with an umbo, when young slightly slimy, when old dry, usually cracked or even split, pale yellowish, cream, whitish or even colourless. Gills grey, later yellowish-brown, dark brown. Stem 3-9x0.3-1.3 cm, thickening towards the base, with a ring, white, grey, fibrous. Flesh thin, soft, white, with a rather sharp smell and an unpleasant taste. Characteristic features: gills grey, when old brown. Grows singly or in small groups. Edible, of low value. Uncommon. The Spring Fieldcap (A. praecox) is very similar; it differs only in that its cap is not cracked (smooth-surfaced) and it appears only in spring. Edible, of low value.

kietoji-guote.habitat: Deciduous forests, especially oak woods with hornbeam and linden, parks
kietoji-guote.features: Fruiting bodies whitish-yellowish, of firm consistency
desc: Fruiting bodies fleshy, medium-sized. Cap 4-8 (12) cm across, domed, later convex, flattened, with a blunt umbo, fleshy, whitish, when old yellowish, ivory-coloured. Gills distant, thick, white, decurrent. Stem 3-6 (8)x1-2 cm, tapering at the base, white, cream, with white fibrils and dots near the gills. Flesh white, firm, without a particular smell, pleasant in taste. Characteristic features: massive white, cream-coloured fruiting bodies, appearing only in deciduous forests, fond of calcareous oak woods. Grows singly or a few fruiting bodies together, likes more open, unshaded places. Warmth-loving. Rare. Edible. Protected.

kislioji-kelmiuke.features: Cap seemingly two-coloured — darker in the centre, paler at the margins
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 3-5 (7) cm across, fading (hygrophanous), not scaly, brownish-yellow, ochre-yellow, yellowish-brown in the centre, honey-coloured, the margins paler. Young gills pale ochre, later greyish-brown, pinkish-brown, brown. Stem 5—7x0.5-0.5 cm, with an indistinct ring, greyish above it, dotted white, below it pinkish-brown, darkening evenly towards the base to dark brown, finely scaly-fibrous, as if roughened. Flesh yellowish, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap fading, not scaly, yellowish-brown. Stem with a small ring. Grows most often in clumps on coniferous and deciduous stumps, windfalls, snags. Edible. A valuable mushroom, in some countries even cultivated artificially. Very common.

kislusis-nuosedis.features: Gills greyish, without a violet tinge, edges toothed
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 3-8 (10) cm across, convex-domed, flattened, slimy, white-fibrous, ochre-yellow, brownish-yellow, the margins with remnants of the white veil. Gills pale cream, later honey-coloured, adnate. Stem 5-8 (10)x1-2 cm, thickening towards the base, white, when old yellowish-brownish, white-fibrous Flesh white, firm, with a faint mushroomy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: cap yellowish-brown, changeable, variable, stem white. Grows singly or in small groups in deciduous forests, sometimes in pine forests. Edible, rare.

kislusis-raudonvirsis.habitat: Mixed, grassy, damp forests, likes the company of birch
kislusis-raudonvirsis.features: Flesh turns red when cut and green at the stem base
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 8-12 cm across, matt, slimy only in damp weather, greyish mottled brown or even blackish-brown. Tubes and pores white, later yellowish, turning brownish when pressed. Stem 10-15x2-3 cm, white, covered with black fibrils. The flesh of the cap and stem quickly turns reddish when cut, eventually fading; at the base of the stem it turns blue, green. Characteristic features: a mushroom of damp, boggy mixed forests and nettle-rich black alder woods. Grows in birch woods and in mixed, deciduous, grassy, boggy forests with birch. Edible, valuable, common, but found less often than the Brown Birch Bolete.

kopine-poniabude.features: Fruiting bodies smaller than those of the Common Stinkhorn
desc: Fruiting bodies smaller than those of the Common Stinkhorn; grows only on sandy dunes. Young fruiting bodies globular, egg-shaped, 3—5 cm across, attached to the substrate by yellowish-pink rhizoids. Exoperidium white, yellowish-pink. Receptacle stem-shaped, 5-12x2-3.5 cm, white, yellowish, with a greenish-violet, blackish-green, slimy head with a very unpleasant smell that is particularly attractive to insects. A head licked clean by insects shows white from afar. Found in the Palanga dunes. Protected.

kopustgalvis-raukslius.features: Whitish, when mature yellowish-brown, cabbage-like mushroom

koraliskasis-trapiadyglis.habitat: On maples, oaks, poplars, at injured parts of trees
desc: Annual. Fruiting bodies 20-40 cm across, branched, fleshy, soft, made up of many coral-like, brittle branches with soft, pointed spines 0.5-1.5 cm long hanging from the underside; when young the spines are white, when old brown. Flesh soft, white, turning brown on drying, like the whole mushroom. Characteristic features: white, coral-like branched fruiting bodies growing on dead wood of deciduous trees. Edible when young, but of low value. Rare, listed in the Red Data Book of Lithuania.

kreivakepuris-piengrybis.habitat: Coniferous forests, especially pine forests Summer, autumn
kreivakepuris-piengrybis.features: Cap with a violet tinge, gills brownish-yellow
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-12 cm across, convex-flattened, when mature irregularly flattened, slightly depressed, slimy, shiny, faintly zoned, fibrous, violet-brown, bluish, greyish-brown. Gills yellowish, brownish-yellow, adnate, with white milk. Stem 3—8x1—3 cm, the colour of the cap. Flesh whitish, later becoming yellowish, thick, firm, with a fruity smell, with white, burning-tasting milk. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies bluish greyish-brown, the milk white, not changing colour. Grows singly or in small groups, especially in pine forests. Not rare. Edible, but of low value, although after boiling in salted water it loses its bitterness.

kriausinis-pumpotaukslis.features: Pear-shaped, turns brown sooner than the Common Puffball
desc: Very similar to the Common Puffball, only the fruiting bodies are smaller, up to 4 cm tall and 2 cm thick, pear-shaped, their peridium (skin) smooth-surfaced or only faintly fibrous. Young ones are white, the flesh white, later turning yellowish, eventually brown. Characteristic features: much smaller than the Common Puffball and smooth-surfaced. Sometimes grows in large groups, most often on rotting stumps, fallen trunks and wood waste. Young ones, while the flesh is white, soft, with a pleasant smell and taste, are edible. Very common; medical scientists have become interested in it.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap 5-10 (12) cm across, becoming flattened as it grows, slightly depressed, margins bent downwards, the cuticle adnate, peeling with difficulty, violet-red in colour, spotted yellowish. Gills crowded, cream, adnate. Stem 3—6x1—3 cm, white, the base tapered. Flesh with a fruity smell, slightly bitter in taste, white, firm. Characteristic features: grows only in deciduous forests. Appears singly or in small groups, likes the company of oak and beech. Edible, not bitter when boiled.

Fruiting bodies medium-sized or small. Cap 3-5 (8) cm across, flattened, slightly irregularly depressed, pale brownish, pinkish-brownish, flesh-coloured. Gills crowded, narrow, whitish, yellowish, when old yellowish-brownish, adnate. Stem 3-9x0.3-0.5 cm, tough, of uniform thickness, pinkish-brown, covered with white down at the base. Flesh thin, tough, yellowish, without a particular smell or taste. Characteristic features: appears in small clumps, the stems literally fused together. Fruiting bodies tough. Grows in groups of a dozen or more fruiting bodies, often on rotting coniferous wood. Edible, of low value. Fairly common.

kuginis-briedziukas.features: Cap margins fused with the stem, colour variable
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Cap grows up to 3-8 cm tall and 2-4 cm across, conical, its surface honeycomb-like, covered with rhomboid pits (alveoli), itself greyish or greenish, sometimes yellowish-brown or even almost black, like a lark standing on tiptoe for flight. Stem 2—7x1—2.5 cm, white, yellowish, with a smooth surface, sometimes faintly wrinkled. Flesh greyish, thin, brittle, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: cap pointed, conical, honeycombed. Grows among grasses, singly or in groups, likes more open places. A valuable edible mushroom, used fresh or dried. Of interest to medical scientists. Common. Protected.

kuokstine-grifole.habitat: At the bases of deciduous trees, especially oaks, lindens, hazels
kuokstine-grifole.features: Many stalked caps with a crimped surface grow from a single stem
desc: A many-capped, annual mushroom, very large, massive, heavy, in rare cases weighing up to 20 kg. The fruiting body has an irregularly shaped central stem from which many stem-like branches grow, each branch topped by a semicircular, fan- or tongue-shaped cap 4-10 cm across. Caps tough, up to 1 cm thick, with wavy margins, concentrically wrinkled, yellowish-grey, older ones greyish-brown in colour. Tubes white, short. Flesh white, with a pleasant smell and a slightly bitter taste. Grows beside stumps or snags, at the root collars of living trees. Causes white rot of wood. Edible, rarely found. Protected.

kvapioji-stirnabude.habitat: Among grasses, mixed, damp, grassy forests, raised bogs, forest margins
kvapioji-stirnabude.features: Fruiting bodies tough, flesh-coloured, with a sharp, musty smell
desc: Fruiting bodies large. Cap 5-15 (20) cm across, when young bell-shaped, later irregularly flattened, hygrophanous, fleshy, fibrous, yellowish-brownish, cream, flesh-coloured. Gills narrow, crowded, cream, adnate. Stem 7-10x1-4 cm, thickening towards the base, fibrous, longitudinally grooved, tough, the colour of the cap. Flesh white, brownish, thick, soft, not bitter, with an unpleasant smell of sweet violet. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies massive, fleshy, tough, growing in large groups. Grows in gloomy, grassy places, several or several dozen fruiting bodies together. Uncommon. Edible. Opinions of it vary, although it is highly praised by the Germans and compared to valuable field mushrooms.

lakuotoji-lakabude.features: Fruiting bodies tough. Gills distant, thick
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1-3 cm, rarely growing up to 3 cm across, finely fibrous or even finely scaly, orange-brown, pinkish-brown or flesh-coloured. Gills distant, thick, adnate. Stem 3-7 (10)x0.3—1.5 cm. Gills and stem the colour of the cap. Flesh with a mushroomy smell, not bitter. Characteristic features: fruiting bodies pinkish-brown, small; appears in all forests of Lithuania, even when other mushrooms are not growing. Appears singly or in small groups. Edible, of low value. Very common.

lapienis-ziurytis.habitat: Rotting wood of deciduous and coniferous trees
lapienis-ziurytis.features: A gelatinous, brown cluster of irregularly intertwined lobes
desc: Fruiting bodies medium-sized. Clusters 3-10 (12) cm across, wrinkled, irregularly plate-like, folded into lobes; when dried out they shrink; brain-like, watery, brown, pinkish-brown, with a violet tinge. Flesh of jelly-like consistency, pale brown, without a particular smell or taste. Grows on fallen deciduous and coniferous trunks, stumps, snags, larger branches. Not afraid of frosts. Not rare. Eaten in some countries; of low value, suitable for adding variety to salads.

lauminis-mazunis.habitat: Meadows, pastures, forest edges, parks, forests
lauminis-mazunis.season: From early spring to late autumn
desc: Fruiting bodies small. Cap 1.3-3 (5) cm across, matt, smooth, yellowish, greyish-yellowish, brownish-yellowish, thin-fleshed. Gills distant, thick, not broad, whitish, yellowish. Stem up to 9 cm long and 0.3-0.7 cm thick, the colour of the cap. Flesh thin, tough, with a pleasant smell and taste. Characteristic features: grows in groups and in rings, forming "fairy rings". Grows in meadows, fallow land, forest edges, forests, parks, gardens, among grasses, on the ground. Very common. A tasty edible mushroom. In some European countries it is eagerly collected for flavouring soups; it is especially praised in German literature.

lelijine-stirnabude.habitat: Damp mixed and coniferous forests, parks, raised bogs
